$comment: CANONICAL CONTRACT for Sparkle's agent permission posture. ONE file, read by BOTH halves'
test suites, so the two hand-written implementations cannot drift apart silently.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Sparkle now writes `permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` into
every managed agent worktree's .claude/settings.local.json, because the approval prompt had
become the fleet's biggest drag: agents were re-blocking once per read-only diagnostic on
COSMETIC triggers (a worktree path containing a space, a `$(...)` substitution, a `sed`
substitution, a `>` redirect, an `&&`). Bypassing the prompt is only safe if the genuinely
destructive commands are still stopped. TWO layers do that, and this file holds the contract
for both. `denyRules` are the Claude Code permission strings Sparkle writes into that same
settings file — coarse, prefix-matched, and blind to compounds. `mustBlock` / `mustAllow` are
the corpora for the PreToolUse guard (worktree-guard.mjs), which lexes the command and is
therefore the layer that catches a destructive command laundered through a compound
(`cd /tmp && rm -rf ~`). There is no third list: a rule lives in `denyRules`, in the guard, or
in both — never in a key that does not exist here.
MEASURED, not assumed (claude 2.1.229, A/B against the real CLI):
bypassPermissions, no deny      -> `rm -f <marker>` RAN (marker deleted). Bypass is real;
headless auto-deny is NOT the explanation.
bypassPermissions + deny rule   -> REFUSED: 'Permission to use Bash with command ... denied'
bypassPermissions + hook exit 2 -> REFUSED: 'PreToolUse:Bash hook error: ...'
So BOTH enforcement layers survive bypassPermissions. Neither is decorative.
THE DISCIPLINE THAT MAKES THIS SAFE: a deny rule has NO approval path — it is a hard refusal a
human cannot click through. So a rule earns its place ONLY if it is unambiguously destructive.
Anything merely risky-looking belongs nowhere near this file; over-blocking here would rebuild
the exact wall we are tearing down, except now with no way through it at all.
Worked examples of rules deliberately REJECTED for ambiguity:
`git reset --hard`  — routine and correct on a feature branch.
`git merge ... main` — merging origin/main INTO your branch is what AGENTS.md tells you to do
when stale. Only a git PUSH to main is unambiguous, so only that is here.
`rm -rf` in general — `rm -rf node_modules` is ordinary. Only catastrophic ROOTS are blocked.
`security:*` blanket— the existing narrow keychain guard already requires all three signals;
a blanket deny would be broader than the shipped policy.

REGRESSION GUARD: the cross-segment judge ran only when NO operands followed -S, so appending one harmless word skipped pipe-to-shell again. The fixture above pinned only the rest-empty spelling, so the suite could not see this one-token-wider variant.

mustBlock.command: env -u A -u B -u C -u D -u E -u F -u G --unset sh -c 'rm -rf /'
mustBlock.why: REGRESSION GUARD, HIGH: a width CAP that truncated the reading list dropped the SHORTEST suffixes — the most plausible real commands — so seven no-op pads pushed the one destructive reading off the end and this was ALLOWED while the unpadded form blocked. A cap an attacker can pad past is not a cap; the budget now refuses instead of truncating.

mustBlock.command: env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env -u env echo hi
mustBlock.why: COVERAGE for the fail-closed budget itself: each alt's command word is literally `env`, so readings multiply per nesting level and pass the budget, while EVERY individual reading resolves to the harmless `echo hi` and fires no rule. So it is ALLOW without the budget and BLOCK with it — the branch is discriminating rather than incidental. Without this the four budget lines could be deleted and all tests still passed.

REGRESSION GUARD, HIGH: the deleter backstop was the ONE non-additive reading — it committed to a single parse and recorded no alternative. Its premise (a deleter in command position is judged) holds for the -exec probe but NOT at top level, where `truncate`/`shred`/`srm`/`unlink` match no rule at all, so refusing to consume re-anchored the parse onto an unjudged word and demoted the real command to an argument.

the same via `rm` itself: at top level the rm rule needs rmIsRecursive, and `sh -c …` carries no -r, so the refused word was judged by nothing

REGRESSION, HIGH: `-type` is a FILTER, not a name. Counting it as narrowing disabled the rule for a command that deletes every regular file under home.

REGRESSION, HIGH: the -exec arm required a RECURSIVE rm, so the widest shape of all was ALLOWED while its `-rf` sibling above was blocked. `-r` only lets rm descend into directories and find has already descended, so a plain rm over `/` deletes every regular file on the system.

`-execdir` is `-exec` run from each file's own directory; it deletes exactly the same set
REGRESSION, HIGH: the tail extractor read only the FIRST -exec clause, so one no-op clause in front hid the delete. find lets the predicate repeat.

`-ok` is `-exec` with a per-file prompt, and the prompt is NOT a guard — `yes | find …` answers every one. The narrowing walk already counted it as command-carrying; only the tail extractor disagreed.

REGRESSION, HIGH: an exact binary-name test reads `env` and misses the `rm` behind it. Enumerating names is only sound once the tail is normalized through the wrapper chain.
the same wrapper laundering via `nice`

REGRESSION GUARD: a `-S`-looking OPERAND of the nested command must not hijack env's option parse. Scanning the whole vector matched `-Sx` after `--` and reported a real `rm -rf` as a non-deleter — worse than the hole the -S handling closed.

the same optional-argument arity, third of three
the ATTACHED form of the optional argument, which is the only form getopt_long accepts for it
`-a` is GNU env's short --argv0 and takes a VALUE; omitted from the short table it walked as a boolean and the S inside its attached value was read as -S — the -uSHELL hijack byte for byte
the separate-word form of the same option, whose value was read as the command word

REGRESSION: the alnum test saw the `x` and called it a name, but `x*` matches zero `x`s — the pattern is `.*` wearing a literal. Optional-quantified atoms must be stripped before asking whether a regex names anything.

REGRESSION, HIGH: `-regex` is BRE on macOS and emacs on GNU, NOT extended — so `\{0,9\}` is the interval and this matches every path. A reader written against ERE ate the backslash form as a literal and counted the `x` as a required name.
the BRE spelling of a quantified-away group

REGRESSION: find's COMMA is the loosest-binding operator and evaluates to its RIGHT operand, so this is always true and deletes every file while containing a perfectly good -name
the same comma, unbracketed

REGRESSION, HIGH: the comma discards the LEFT operand's VALUE but still EVALUATES it, so -delete runs over / while the last segment names something. Reading only the last segment was a bypass of its own.

the same left-of-comma action, via -exec. The `+` spelling and not `\;`: a `;` is a shell command separator, so that variant is split before the find logic ever sees the comma and would pin nothing here.
REGRESSION the flat `-o` scan used to catch: splitting on the comma FIRST drops the whole `-false -o -delete` half, and -false forces -delete over every file

REGRESSION: POSIX fnmatch reads a `]` in the FIRST position as a MEMBER of the class, not the terminator. A `\[[^\]]*\]` strip closes at that `]` and leaves `a-z]*` behind as apparent literal text — the class bypass, spelled with one extra character.
the negated spelling of the same leading-`]` class

REGRESSION: a POSIX `[:class:]` sub-expression holds a `]` that ends the SUB-EXPRESSION, not the class. Closing there left `x]*` behind, so the `x` counted as a name. The leak needs a member AFTER the sub-expression — `[[:alpha:]]*` strips to non-alnum residue either way, which is why the obvious spelling read as covering it.
the same early close on the regex path, where the residual `x` is then read as a required atom

REGRESSION, HIGH: an UNTERMINATED sub-expression is not a sub-expression — fnmatch rewinds and reads the `[` as an ordinary member. Refusing from inside the class returned the same -1 the glob path reads as `literal [`, so the strip re-scanned, took a SHORTER class, and left `[a-z` behind as literal text. This is `'[a-z]*'` re-opened by adding two characters.
the same malformed sub-expression with a member before it, and a class NAME that merely lacks its `:]`
the `[.coll.]` spelling of the same unterminated sub-expression
and the `[=equiv=]` spelling

mustAllow.command:
cat > note.txt <<'EOF'
git push --force origin main
rm -rf /
EOF
mustAllow.why: REGRESSION, found the hard way: a heredoc BODY is data being written, not commands being run — the same distinction as a quoted string, which the lexer cannot see because the body is newline-separated. This guard refused a real edit whose script text merely QUOTED a destructive command.
a here-STRING is quoted data on one line

mustBlockMultiline.why: REGRESSION, HIGH: a `(?!<)` lookahead does not exclude `<<<` — the engine retries one character later and matches at the SECOND `<`, so the here-string opened a heredoc named `foo` and every following line, including this `rm -rf /`, was discarded as body. The single-line here-string case could never catch it.
a QUOTED mention of the operator must not open a body — the stripper has to be quoting-aware, not just anchored

REGRESSION, HIGH: the heredoc scanner was quoting-aware PER LINE ONLY, so a shell string spanning lines left it believing the next line was unquoted — a `<<WORD` inside that string opened a body and discarded every following line, this `rm -rf /` included, before the lexer saw it. Quote state now threads across lines.
